module_title: Planning, Budgeting, and Sustaining Preservation Projects

lessons.title: Conducting a Building Condition Survey
lessons.body: A building condition survey is a systematic inspection to record what is wrong and what is at risk. Start by gathering basic tools: a notebook, pencil, tape measure (5m), torch, camera or phone, and a simple checklist. Walk the building from top to bottom. Check the roof for missing tiles, cracks, or rusted sheets. Look at walls for damp patches, peeling paint, and structural cracks wider than 3mm. Inspect foundations for exposed footings or erosion. Test doors and windows for rot or sticking. Note any sagging ceilings or floors. Take photos of each problem and write its location (e.g., 'north wall, near window'). Rate each issue: urgent (fix within 1 month), important (fix within 6 months), or monitor (check yearly). For example, a leaking roof in Ghana's rainy season is urgent; a small crack in a storeroom wall may be monitored. If you lack expertise, invite a local mason or engineer to help for a small fee. Record everything in a simple table: item, condition, action needed, estimated cost. This survey becomes your baseline. Repeat it every 6 months to track changes. Without a survey, you risk wasting money on the wrong repairs. Involving local peopleâlike the caretaker or eldersâhelps you spot hidden issues. Keep the report in a safe place; it will guide your budget and maintenance calendar.

lessons.title: Estimating Costs and Sourcing Materials Locally
lessons.body: Estimating costs means figuring out how much money and materials you need before you start. First, list every repair from your condition survey. For each, decide the materials: cement, sand, timber, nails, paint, roofing sheets, etc. Then measure quantities. For example, to plaster a 10m x 3m wall, you need about 0.5 cubic meters of sand and 5 bags of cement. Check local prices at hardware stores, markets, or from artisans. In Kenya, a bag of cement might cost 600-800 KES; in Nigeria, 4,000-5,000 NGN. Always get three quotes. Sourcing locally saves transport costs and supports the community. Look for second-hand materials: salvaged bricks, roofing sheets, or timber from demolished buildings. But inspect for qualityâavoid termite-eaten wood or cracked tiles. Consider using earth blocks, bamboo, or thatch if they are traditional and cheap. For labour, ask local masons and carpenters for daily rates (e.g., 2,000-5,000 KES per day). Add 10-15% contingency for price changes or hidden damage. Keep a simple budget sheet: item, quantity, unit price, total. Compare with your available funds. If costs exceed funds, prioritise urgent repairs and phase the work. Buy materials in bulk if you have storage. Negotiate discounts for cash payments. Record every purchase with receipts. This discipline prevents running out of money halfway.

lessons.title: Creating a Maintenance Calendar
lessons.body: A maintenance calendar is a schedule of routine tasks to keep your building in good condition. It prevents small problems from becoming big, expensive ones. Start by listing recurring tasks: cleaning gutters, checking roof after storms, repainting every 3-5 years, servicing doors and windows, clearing drains, and inspecting foundations. For each task, decide frequency: weekly, monthly, quarterly, or yearly. For example, in West Africa's rainy season (April-September), check the roof and gutters every two weeks. In dry season, water the foundation if it's cracking. Assign a responsible personâmaybe a caretaker or volunteerâand write their name on the calendar. Use a simple wall chart or a notebook. Mark dates for inspections: e.g., '1st Saturday: roof check' or 'End of month: clean drains'. Include seasonal tasks: before rains, clear drainage; after rains, check for leaks. Also schedule major surveys every 6 months. Budget for maintenance: set aside a small amount monthly (e.g., 5,000 KES) for minor repairs. If you have a committee, review the calendar quarterly and adjust. Train the caretaker to spot issues early. A calendar turns preservation into a habit, not a crisis. Post it where everyone can see. Involving local youth or women's groups can share the workload and build skills.

lessons.title: Training and Involving Local Workers
lessons.body: Local workers are your greatest asset for preservation. They know the building, the materials, and the climate. But they may lack specific skills in historic repair. Start by identifying willing people: masons, carpenters, roofers, and handy youth. Organise short training sessionsâ2-3 hoursâled by an experienced artisan or a preservation officer. Focus on practical techniques: mixing lime mortar instead of cement for old walls, repairing thatch, or treating timber for termites. Use local materials and tools. For example, show how to make a mud plaster with clay, sand, and straw. Train in safety: wearing gloves, using ladders correctly, and handling tools. Emphasise gentle repairs: avoid harsh chemicals or heavy machinery that damage old fabric. Pay workers fairlyâeither daily wages or in-kind (food, materials). Involve the community in decision-making: hold a meeting to discuss the plan and get their input. This builds ownership and ensures maintenance continues after the project. Encourage apprenticeships: pair young learners with skilled elders. Document the training with photos and notes. After training, create a small team responsible for different tasks. Recognise their work publiclyâa certificate or a community announcement. When local people are invested, they protect the building. They will notice problems early and fix them quickly. This approach also keeps money in the local economy.

lessons.title: Funding Options: Grants, Loans, and Community Contributions
lessons.body: Funding a preservation project requires mixing sources. Grants are free money from donors, NGOs, or government heritage funds. Examples: UNESCO World Heritage Fund, African World Heritage Fund, or local cultural trusts. To apply, you need a clear plan, budget, and photos. Write a simple proposal: what you will do, why it matters, how much you need. Deadlines are strict; apply early. Loans from banks or microfinance institutions must be repaid with interest. Use loans only for income-generating repairsâlike turning a historic building into a guesthouse or market. Interest rates in Africa can be 10-30% per year, so calculate carefully. Community contributions are powerful: cash, labour, materials, or food. Organise a fundraising eventâa football match, a dance, or a raffle. Ask local businesses to donate cement or paint. Set up a bank account with two signatories for transparency. Keep records of every donation. Combine sources: a grant for materials, community labour for work, and a small loan for tools. For example, a project in Tanzania raised 2 million TZS from a local harambee, plus a 1 million TZS grant. Always report back to donors with photos and receipts. Transparency builds trust for future funding. Avoid relying on one source; diversify. Start small and build a track record. Partner with a registered NGO to access bigger grants.

lessons.title: Final Project: Develop a Preservation Plan for a Local Building
lessons.body: Your final project is to create a complete preservation plan for a building in your community. Choose a building that mattersâa mosque, church, school, clinic, or historic home. It should be at risk or in need of care. Follow these steps: 1) Conduct a condition survey using the methods from Lesson 1. Take photos and note urgent repairs. 2) Estimate costs and source materials locally (Lesson 2). Get quotes and list quantities. 3) Create a maintenance calendar with tasks and responsible persons (Lesson 3). 4) Plan training for local workers (Lesson 4). 5) Identify funding options: grants, loans, and community contributions (Lesson 5). Write a 2-3 page plan with sections: Building Description, Survey Findings, Budget, Maintenance Schedule, Training Plan, and Funding Strategy. Include a simple map or sketch. Set a timeline: short-term (0-3 months), medium (3-12 months), long-term (1-3 years). Present your plan to a community meeting or a local committee. Ask for feedback and adjust. Then implement the first urgent repair as a pilot. Keep records of everything: receipts, photos, attendance. After 6 months, review and update the plan. This project teaches you to turn knowledge into action. A good plan is realistic, uses local resources, and involves the community. It should be a living documentânot filed away. Share it with others so they can learn. By preserving one building, you inspire preservation of others.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Planning, Budgeting, and Sustaining Preservation Projects

Across Africa, heritage buildings â from Swahili coral-stone houses on the East African coast to Sudanese mud-brick mosques, Asante shrines, and colonial-era warehouses â share a hard economic reality: they rarely survive on sentiment alone. They survive when someone can answer three questions with numbers and a calendar: What condition is the building in? What will it cost to keep it standing? Who pays, and when? This Practical Reference module gives you the working tools to answer those questions, whether you are a small contractor, a heritage trust officer, a municipal works manager, or a community leader preparing a preservation plan for a local building.

Treat a preservation project like any other asset-management business. A building that is surveyed, costed, scheduled, staffed, and funded is a building that stays in use. A building that is only loved is a building that collapses in the next heavy rain.

1. Conducting a Building Condition Survey

A condition survey is your balance sheet of physical assets. Walk the building systematically and record defects by element: foundations, walls, roof, floors, openings, services. For each defect note location, extent, severity (1â5), and likely cause. Photograph everything with a scale reference and a date stamp. In African contexts, pay special attention to:

  • Water and damp: the single biggest killer of historic fabric. Check roof valleys, gutters, rising damp in mud-brick or coral rag, and termite trails.
  • Biological attack: termites, wood-boring beetles, mould, and vegetation roots in masonry.
  • Structural movement: cracks wider than 3 mm, bulging walls, differential settlement near trees or seasonal water courses.
  • Material loss: eroded mortar, spalled render, corroded iron ties, degraded thatch or shingles.
  • Use and safety: occupancy load, fire escape, electrical condition, and accessibility.

2. Estimating Costs and Sourcing Materials Locally

Cost estimation for preservation is not the same as new construction. You are buying repair, not replacement. Build your estimate from the survey's quantities, then price them with local rates. Three cost categories matter:

  • Labour: skilled masons, carpenters, thatchers, and unskilled helpers. In many African markets, labour can be 40â60% of a preservation budget.
  • Materials: lime, sand, coral rag, timber, iron, thatch, clay. Source locally where possible â it lowers cost, reduces transport emissions, and matches historic fabric.
  • Contingency: 10â20% for hidden defects, currency swings, and weather delays.

Local sourcing is both a business decision and a preservation decision. A lime putty made from locally burned limestone behaves more like historic mortar than a bagged cement mix. A carpenter in the same town can cut replacement timber to match the original. Build a supplier list with two or three options per material so you are not stranded when one source fails.

Table 1. Indicative preservation cost breakdown (percentage of project budget)
Cost categoryTypical shareNotes for African projects
Skilled labour25â35%Masons, carpenters, thatchers; often scarce, so budget for training
Unskilled labour15â25%Local hire builds community buy-in and reduces cost
Local materials20â30%Lime, sand, timber, thatch, stone; transport can add 10â20%
Imported/specialist materials5â10%Consolidants, specialist fixings, conservation-grade products
Contingency10â20%Hidden defects, weather, currency, security
Professional fees & permits5â10%Surveyor, engineer, heritage approval

Sources: Adapted from UNESCO, Managing Disaster Risks for World Heritage (2010), and the Aga Khan Trust for Culture's project cost reporting (aktc.org).

3. Creating a Maintenance Calendar

Most preservation failures are maintenance failures. A calendar converts good intentions into recurring tasks with owners and deadlines. Align it with the local climate: before the rains, during the dry season, after harvest, and before the tourist high season.

Table 2. Sample annual maintenance calendar for a historic building in a two-season African climate
PeriodTaskResponsibleBudget line
Pre-rains (1â2 months before)Clear gutters, check roof, seal cracks, prune treesCaretaker + masonRoutine maintenance
RainsMonitor leaks, damp, termite activity; emergency repairs onlyCaretakerContingency
Post-rainsFull condition walk, photograph defects, update surveySurveyor + caretakerSurvey budget
Dry seasonRepoint mortar, treat timber, repaint, replace thatchSkilled masonsCapital repair
AnnuallyReview insurance, permits, funding, and 5-year planManager/trusteesAdministration

Sources: Based on ICCROMâUNESCO, Risk Preparedness: A Management Manual for World Cultural Heritage (1998), and National Trust maintenance-planning practice.

4. Training and Involving Local Workers

Preservation is a skills business. Every project should leave behind more capable people than it found. Practical steps:

  • Pair an experienced conservation mason or carpenter with 2â3 local apprentices for the duration of the works.
  • Run short (1â3 day) workshops on lime mortar, timber repair, thatch, or damp diagnosis, open to local contractors.
  • Write simple, illustrated method statements in the local language and leave them with the building.
  • Pay fairly and on time â this is how you keep good workers and build a local preservation labour market.
  • Document before-and-after photographs; they are evidence for future funding bids.

5. Funding Options: Grants, Loans, and Community Contributions

No single source sustains a building. A resilient funding plan stacks three or four streams:

  • Grants: heritage trusts, embassies, the African World Heritage Fund, UNESCO participation programme, and private foundations. Usually project-based, not recurrent â use for capital repair, not for the caretaker's monthly wage.
  • Loans: commercial or microfinance loans can fund income-generating uses (cafÃ©, guesthouse, workspace) that then repay the loan and fund maintenance. Requires a real business plan.
  • Community contributions: cash, labour, materials, or in-kind use of land and equipment. Strong in rural areas; must be recorded and recognised.
  • Earned income: tours, events, rentals, parking, filming fees. The most sustainable stream if the building is in active use.
  • Government: municipal maintenance budgets, tourism levies, and national heritage funds.
â  SAFETY WARNING â Read before any site work

Preservation sites are hazardous. Never enter a building with active structural movement, sagging roof, or unstable upper floors without a qualified engineer's clearance. Assume asbestos, lead paint, and bat or rodent droppings may be present in older buildings â use appropriate PPE (respirator, gloves, eye protection) and follow local hazardous-waste rules. Scaffolding must be erected by trained persons and inspected daily. In malaria- and dengue-endemic areas, use repellent and cover water containers. Do not allow untrained volunteers to demolish, prop, or work at height. If in doubt, stop work and get professional advice.

6. Final Project: Develop a Preservation Plan for a Local Building

Your final deliverable is a single document (10â20 pages) covering: condition survey summary with photographs; prioritised defect list with severity; itemised budget with local rates and contingency; 12-month maintenance calendar; training and local-employment plan; funding strategy with at least three income streams; and a monitoring schedule. Present it to the building owner, community, or trust. A plan that is not presented and adopted is not a plan â it is a draft.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Survey completed element-by-element, with dated photographs and a severity rating for every defect.
  2. Budget built from measured quantities and local rates, with 10â20% contingency.
  3. At least two local suppliers identified for each key material.
  4. 12-month maintenance calendar agreed, with named responsibilities and budget lines.
  5. Training plan in place: apprentices paired with skilled workers, method statements left on site.
  6. Funding stack includes at least three streams â grant, earned income, and community or government contribution.
  7. Safety plan and PPE in place before any work starts; engineer's clearance for structural work.
  8. Plan presented, adopted, and reviewed annually with before-and-after documentation.

Further Reading (free official sources)

  • UNESCO World Heritage Centre â Managing Disaster Risks for World Heritage: whc.unesco.org/en/activities/630/
  • ICCROM â Risk Preparedness: A Management Manual for World Cultural Heritage: iccrom.org/publication/risk-preparedness
  • Getty Conservation Institute â Building Condition Assessment resources: getty.edu/conservation/publications_resources/
  • African World Heritage Fund â funding and capacity programmes: awhf.net
  • ICOMOS â Illustrated Glossary on Stone Deterioration Patterns: icomos.org/publications/monuments_and_sites/

quiz.q: What is the first step in conducting a building condition survey?
options: A) Gather basic tools and a checklist
quiz.explanation: You need tools and a checklist to systematically record problems.

quiz.q: Which of these is an urgent repair?
options: A) A small crack in a storeroom wall
B) A leaking roof during rainy season
C) Peeling paint in a hallway
quiz.explanation: A leaking roof can cause rapid structural damage and must be fixed within a month.

quiz.q: How often should you repeat a building condition survey?
quiz.explanation: Regular surveys track changes and catch new problems early.

quiz.q: Why is it important to involve local people in the survey?
options: A) They can spot hidden issues
B) They will pay for repairs
quiz.explanation: Locals know the building's history and can identify problems outsiders miss.

quiz.q: What should you record for each problem found?
options: C) The name of the person who caused it
quiz.explanation: Location, photo, and rating help prioritise and plan repairs.

quiz.q: What is the first step in estimating costs?
options: B) List every repair from the survey
quiz.explanation: You need a list of repairs to know what materials and labour are needed.

quiz.q: How many quotes should you get for materials?
quiz.explanation: Getting three quotes helps you find the best price and avoid overpaying.

quiz.q: Which material can be sourced locally to save money?
quiz.explanation: Salvaged bricks are often cheap or free and reduce transport costs.

quiz.q: What percentage of contingency should you add to your budget?
quiz.explanation: A 10-15% contingency covers price changes or hidden damage.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep receipts for all purchases?
options: A) To show donors and track spending
quiz.explanation: Receipts provide accountability and help you stay within budget.

quiz.q: What is a maintenance calendar?
options: B) A schedule of routine tasks
quiz.explanation: It schedules recurring tasks to prevent small problems from growing.

quiz.q: How often should you check the roof during rainy season?
quiz.explanation: Frequent checks during rains catch leaks early.

quiz.q: Who should be responsible for maintenance tasks?
options: A) A named person like a caretaker
quiz.explanation: Assigning a specific person ensures tasks get done.

quiz.q: What should you do before the rainy season?
options: A) Clear drainage and check roof
quiz.explanation: Clearing drains and checking roofs prevents water damage.

quiz.q: How often should you review the maintenance calendar?
quiz.explanation: Quarterly reviews allow adjustments for seasonal changes.

quiz.q: What is the best way to train local workers?
options: B) Short practical sessions with an experienced artisan
quiz.explanation: Hands-on training with a skilled artisan is effective and affordable.

quiz.q: Which technique is suitable for old walls?
quiz.explanation: Lime mortar is softer and allows old walls to breathe.

quiz.q: Why should you pay workers fairly?
options: A) To keep them motivated and build trust
quiz.explanation: Fair pay ensures quality work and community support.

quiz.q: What is an apprenticeship?
options: A) Pairing young learners with skilled elders
quiz.explanation: Apprenticeships transfer skills and keep knowledge alive.

quiz.q: How can you recognise local workers' contributions?
options: A) Give certificates or public announcements
quiz.explanation: Recognition boosts morale and encourages continued involvement.

quiz.q: What is a grant?
quiz.explanation: Grants do not need to be repaid.

quiz.q: Which of these is a community contribution?
quiz.explanation: Community contributions include labour, materials, or cash from locals.

quiz.q: What should you do before applying for a grant?
options: A) Write a clear plan and budget
quiz.explanation: Donors require a detailed proposal to assess your project.

quiz.q: Why is transparency important in funding?
options: A) It builds trust for future funding
C) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: Transparency with donors and community ensures accountability and support.

quiz.q: What is a good way to raise community funds?
quiz.explanation: Events like football matches or raffles bring people together and raise money.

quiz.q: What is the final project in this module?
options: A) Develop a preservation plan for a local building
quiz.explanation: The project applies all lessons to a real building in your community.

quiz.q: How long should your preservation plan be?
quiz.explanation: A concise plan covering key sections is sufficient and practical.

quiz.q: What should you include in your preservation plan?
options: A) Survey findings, budget, maintenance schedule, training, funding
quiz.explanation: All these sections ensure a comprehensive plan.

quiz.q: What should you do after presenting your plan to the community?
options: A) Ask for feedback and adjust
quiz.explanation: Community feedback improves the plan and builds ownership.

quiz.q: Why is a preservation plan a 'living document'?
options: A) It should be reviewed and updated regularly
C) It is written on paper
quiz.explanation: Regular reviews keep the plan relevant as conditions change.
